newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia/Pacific import reliance for kerosene growing.
newsitem.headline: Asia/Pacific import reliance for kerosene growing.

text.p: The Asia-Pacific region's reliance on net imports of jet/kerosene is likely to fall slightly in the next two or three years, but import deficits will widen after 2000, energy analyst Nancy Yamaguchi said on Wednesday.
The imports can easily be sourced out of the Middle East for now, but from 2010 demand could just outpace Middle East supply, she told Reuters in an interview.

"What we are finding is that all the regions, except Southeast Asia, are net importers of jet from now until well into the future and even Southeast Asian exports will begin to dwindle by 2010," she said on the sidelines of the AviaFuels 1997 conference in Singapore.
"Imports have to rise. There is not enough firmly planned capacity additions and refinery margins do not warrant people to rush out and build a refinery anyway," she said.
Broad-based economic expansion, but also expanding air travel, will drive demand for jet/kerosene in coming years.
Asia as a whole is the power house of world energy demand and by 2000 is expected to be the biggest consuming region on earth, surpassing North America in its energy needs.

Yamaguchi, president of Trans-Energy Research Associates of the United States, forecast Asian/Pacific jet/kerosene imports would rise to 230,000 barrels per day (bpd) in 2000 from 165,000 in 1997, before rising to 270,000 in 2005 and 460,000 in 2010.
But different areas of the region will experience different profiles in their demand and supply balance for jet/kerosene.
Southeast Asia, including Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, Burma, Philippines, Singapore and Thailand, will remain the only region with net exports, although they will dwindle in time.

Yamaguchi said Southeast Asia jet/kerosene production would rise to 700,000 bpd by 2005 from 500,000 in 1997. Exports from the region were just less than 100,000 bpd currently, but that would fall to around 20,000 bpd in 2010.
The other regions would remain net importers of jet/kerosene.

Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea, will see imports double from now to 2000 to 24,000 bpd, reaching 34,000 bpd in 2010, even as production rises to aorund 130,000 bpd from just under 100,000 bpd currently, Yamaguchi said.
South Asia -- India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka -- faces growing imports, but they are likely to be cheaper because the region is closer to the Middle East, she said.
Yamaguchi forecast production of jet/kerosene would rise to 500,000 bpd in South Asia by 2010 from just more than 200,000 bpd now.
However, the volume of imports would remain steady at 150,000 bpd until 2000 before growing strongly in the next decade to 300,000 bpd in 2010, she said.

Imports into East Asia, including China, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea, were expected to dip in 1997 to around 100,000 bpd following refinery expansions in South Korea. But from 2000 imports are expected to grow steadily to 150,000 bpd by 2010.
Middle East exports currently outpace Asia demand by around 120,000 bpd, but Yamaguchi forecast the gap would close steadily so that by 2010 Asia demand would just outpace Middle East supplies.
That could signal higher prices as imports will have to be sourced from other continents, she said.
